h1: An owner's engineer for a brewery project
title: An Owner's Engineer for a Brewery | Craft Beer School
desc: What an owner's engineer does on a brewery build: reviewing scope, watching the supplier, checking commissioning and protecting the owner's interests.
teaser: The supplier knows the equipment. The owner knows the business. Someone has to stand between the two and read the drawings.
standfirst: An owner's engineer is an independent technical adviser who works for you, not the supplier. This guide explains the role, when it pays off and what to expect from it.
sections:
On a brewery build the owner is usually new to brewery construction. The supplier builds breweries for a living. That gap in knowledge is the reason owners get surprised late in a project.

An owner's engineer closes the gap. This person reads the specification, questions the drawings, visits the fabrication shop or joins by video call, attends commissioning and tells you in plain language whether the plant is as agreed. Their only client is you.

The role differs from the supplier's project manager. The supplier's manager keeps the schedule on the supplier's terms. The owner's engineer keeps the plant on the terms you signed.

There are four points in a project where independent review changes outcomes.

  • Before you sign: does the scope match the plant you need? Is anything missing?
  • During design: do vessel sizes, pipe runs, drains and access make sense for daily cleaning and maintenance?
  • During fabrication and delivery: is the build to specification? Are welds, finishes and instruments as agreed?
  • At commissioning: do water tests, cleaning trials and trial brews prove the plant works?

Each of these is cheaper to fix early. A tank that has no room for a person to reach the manway is easy to spot on a drawing. It is miserable to discover after installation.

Good review is specific. Typical checks ask three questions. Does the brewhouse size match the fermentation capacity, so the cellar is neither starved nor idle? Is the cold side designed for cleaning, with no dead legs where beer can sit? Are utilities sized for peak demand rather than average demand?

Utilities deserve extra attention. Refrigeration capacity, steam or hot water supply, compressed air quality and electrical load are easy to under-size when a supplier quotes the equipment but leaves utilities as the owner's problem. In a hot climate, refrigeration shortfalls show up in the first summer.

Packaging is another frequent weak point. The line may run at its rated speed on a good day. Whether it keeps that speed with your container mix and your crew is a separate question.

Commissioning is where a paper plant becomes a working one. The engineer should help write the test plan before the supplier arrives: pressure tests, water runs, cleaning cycle verification, temperature control checks and then trial brews that measure efficiency and losses.

Insist that results go in a written acceptance record. Anything the plant fails to do should appear as a snag list with dates. Payments should follow the list. Our guide on what a turnkey contract should cover explains how handover tests connect to payment.
When you may not need one

A very small plant bought from an established supplier, installed by a team you trust, may not need full-time oversight. A short review of the scope and a visit at commissioning could be enough.

The larger and more bespoke the project, the stronger the case. Owners funding a plant from a loan or from investors often also want independent confirmation that money was spent on what was agreed. A business health report or a project review can serve that purpose.

We act as an owner's engineer on brewery projects, working remotely by video call and shared documents with site visits by arrangement. Rahul Baliyan leads on the technical side: brewhouse, cellar, utilities and commissioning. Ankur Napa leads on quality systems, costing and data.

We tell you what we see. If the equipment is fine and the plan is sound we say so. We do not name clients or promise outcomes. Licensing and statutory approvals stay with you and your adviser, since alcohol is a state subject in India and requirements differ between states and change.
Questions an owner's engineer asks first

Some of the most useful questions are simple. Where does the wort go if a pump fails? How do you drain this tank completely? How does a person climb to this valve with a hose in hand? What happens to the plant if the power drops for ten minutes in the middle of a brew?

Another question is who services each instrument. Temperature probes, pressure gauges and flow meters drift. A plant with no calibration plan will slowly lose control of its process without anyone noticing.

Ask for the spare parts list too. Which parts wear out in the first year? How fast can the supplier deliver them? A pump seal that takes six weeks to arrive can stop a brewery.
faqs: Is an owner's engineer the same as a project manager?
Not quite. A project manager runs the schedule and budget. An owner's engineer checks that the plant is technically what you bought. Some projects need both.
Much of it can: reviewing contracts, drawings and test records by video call. Site visits are best at key points such as factory inspection and commissioning.
Does the role replace the supplier's own testing?
No. It adds an independent check. The supplier still tests its own work. You hold both sides to the written acceptance criteria.
